[[File:Claudius Gros 2016.png|thumb|right|Claudius Gros 2016]]
'''Claudius Gros''' (born 18 February 1961 in Mainz, Germany) is a German physicist. He is a professor of theoretical physics in [[Goethe University Frankfurt]] since 2005. He specializes in [[computational neuroscience]]s and [[complex systems theory]].<ref>{{Cite web |title=Goethe-Universität — Institut für Theoretische Physik |url=https://www.goethe-university-frankfurt.de/66535545/Workgroup_Gros |access-date=2023-10-06 |website=www.goethe-university-frankfurt.de}}</ref>

== Career ==
Finishing his studies in physics 1985 at the [[ETH Zurich|ETH Zürich]] with a thesis on [[Heavy fermion material|heavy Fermions]], Gros continued for a [[Doctor of Philosophy|PhD]] in theoretical [[solid-state physics]]. Using projected [[wave function]]s, as introduced originally by [[Martin Gutzwiller]], he and his advisor, [[Thomas Maurice Rice]], were able to predict [[unconventional superconductor|d-wave superconductivity]] for [[high temperature superconductivity|high-temperature superconductors]].<ref name="Gros 1989 pp. 53–88">{{cite journal | last=Gros | first=Claudius | title=Physics of projected wavefunctions | journal=Annals of Physics | publisher=Elsevier BV | volume=189 | issue=1 | year=1989 | issn=0003-4916 | doi=10.1016/0003-4916(89)90077-8 | pages=53–88| bibcode=1989AnPhy.189...53G }}</ref>

From 1988-1990, Gros worked with [[Steven M. Girvin]] and [[Allan H. MacDonald]] at the [[Indiana University]] in [[Bloomington, Indiana]]. He then spent time at [[Technical University of Dortmund|Dortmund University]].  In 1999, he joined [[Saarland University]] as professor of [[theoretical physics]].  In 2005, he moved to [[Goethe University Frankfurt]].  Gros now works in [[complex systems]] theory, focusing on [[complex adaptive system]]s relevant to the [[neuroscience]]s.  His lecture course on the subject has seen four editions.<ref name="Gros 2013 p. ">{{cite book | last=Gros | first=Claudius | title=Complex and adaptive dynamical systems : a primer | publisher=Springer | publication-place=Berlin New York | year=2013 | isbn=978-3-642-36586-7 | oclc=841465413 | page=}}</ref><ref>{{Cite journal |last=Feldman |first=David P. |date=2009-07-01 |title=Books: ''Complex and Adaptive Dynamical Systems: A Primer'' |journal=Physics Today |volume=62 |issue=7 |pages=58–59 |doi=10.1063/1.3177233 |issn=0031-9228|doi-access=free |arxiv=0807.4838 }}</ref> In 2016, Gros published a novel.<ref name="Gros 2016 p. ">{{cite book | last=Gros | first=Claudius | title=Mageia Das Buch der Farben | publisher=tredition | publication-place=Hamburg | year=2016 | isbn=978-3-7345-4847-5 | oclc=968234326 | language=de | page=}}</ref> He is married to physicist [[Roser Maria Valentí|Roser Valentí]].

==Genesis Project==
In 2016 Gros studied the feasibility of a low-cost [[interstellar probe|interstellar mission]], aiming to establish a [[biosphere]] of [[unicellular organism]]s on otherwise only transiently [[Planetary habitability|habitable]] [[exoplanet]]s, fast-forwarding [[evolution]] potentially by several billion years.<ref name="Gros2016">{{cite journal|last1=Gros|first1=Claudius|title=Developing ecospheres on transiently habitable planets: the genesis project|journal=Astrophysics and Space Science|volume=361|issue=10|year=2016|page=324|issn=0004-640X|doi=10.1007/s10509-016-2911-0|arxiv=1608.06087|bibcode=2016Ap&SS.361..324G|doi-access=free}}</ref> The long mission duration would imply, according to Gros, that the Genesis Project would not have any tangible benefit for humanity. The initial acceleration could be achieved by [[laser propulsion]], akin to that envisioned by the [[Breakthrough Starshot]] project, with passive deceleration at the target using [[magnetic sail]]s.  Overall, the probe would weight about 1.5 tons and travel at 0.3 percent of the [[speed of light]].<ref name="Romero 2017">{{cite web | last=Romero | first=James | title=Should we seed life through the cosmos using laser-driven ships? | website=New Scientist | date=13 November 2017 | url=https://www.newscientist.com/article/2153165-should-we-seed-life-through-the-cosmos-using-laser-driven-ships/ | access-date=12 January 2022}}</ref>  An on-board miniaturized gene laboratory would [[artificial cell|synthesize]] the microbes.<ref name="Callaway pp. 557–558">{{cite journal | last=Callaway | first=Ewen | title='Minimal' cell raises stakes in race to harness synthetic life | journal=Nature | publisher=Springer Science and Business Media LLC | volume=531 | issue=7596 | date=24 March 2016 | issn=0028-0836 | doi=10.1038/531557a | pages=557–558| pmid=27029256 | bibcode=2016Natur.531..557C | s2cid=4457074 | doi-access=free }}</ref>

The [[precambrian]] biosphere established by the Genesis probe would evolve subsequently on its own, potentially to [[Multicellular organism|complex lifeforms]]. The concept of the Genesis Project carries a series of fundamental ethical and philosophical aspects, which have been discussed in the media.
